properties.name: Rome
properties.one_line: Paul's letter to the Romans reached this community around 57 CE, and by 117 CE Rome held one of the empire's largest Christian populations. Nero blamed the group for the great fire of 64 CE and executed many in his own gardens. Ignatius of Antioch wrote ahead to Rome's believers in 107 CE, begging them not to intervene in his coming martyrdom. Its catacombs would later preserve some of the earliest surviving Christian burial art in the city.
properties.image_credit: Good Shepherd fresco, Catacomb of Priscilla, Rome · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Early Christian fresco of the Good Shepherd in the Catacomb of Priscilla, Rome

properties.name: Antioch
properties.one_line: Antioch's believers were the first anywhere called Christians, a name the Book of Acts records taking hold in this city. Peter and Paul both preached here before it became a missionary base for the wider Mediterranean. Ignatius served as its bishop until Trajan condemned him around 107 CE and shipped him to Rome for execution. His seven surviving letters, written en route, give historians their clearest window into a Christian community of this exact period.
properties.image_credit: Mosaic from Antioch on the Orontes, 115-150 CE, Louvre Museum · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman-period mosaic excavated at ancient Antioch, dated close to 117 CE

properties.name: Alexandria
properties.one_line: Tradition holds that Mark the Evangelist founded Alexandria's church around 42 CE, preaching among the city's huge Jewish population. By 117 CE the community stayed small and out of public view, decades before producing theologians like Origen. The Kitos War tore through the city in 115-117 CE as Jewish and Greek residents fought street battles that Rome's general Quintus Marcius Turbo took months to suppress. Alexandria's Christians later traced their bishops back to this decade.
properties.image_credit: Roman-period Alexandria, Kom el-Dikka · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman-era ruins in Alexandria, Egypt

properties.name: Corinth
properties.one_line: Paul spent eighteen months building this congregation around 50 CE, drawing converts from Corinth's dockworkers, merchants, and freed slaves. His two surviving letters to the community argue over lawsuits, factions, and who could eat meat sold near pagan temples. Corinth's mixed Roman colony setting made it one of the best-documented Christian communities of the first century. By 117 CE its members had already weathered a generation of internal disputes.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Apollo, ancient Corinth · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the Temple of Apollo at ancient Corinth

properties.name: Ephesus
properties.one_line: Paul preached in Ephesus for roughly two years around 53-55 CE, long enough to provoke a riot from silversmiths who sold statuettes of Artemis. The city's Christians later received a letter in the Book of Revelation warning they had abandoned their first love. Ignatius of Antioch wrote to them around 107 CE while under armed guard, praising their unity around a single bishop. Ephesus ranked alongside Rome, Antioch, and Alexandria as one of early Christianity's four major centers.
properties.image_credit: Great Theatre of Ephesus · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The Great Theatre at ancient Ephesus

properties.name: Smyrna
properties.one_line: Smyrna's Christians received one of the seven letters in the Book of Revelation, promising a martyr's crown to the faithful. Around 107 CE, Ignatius of Antioch stopped here and befriended its young bishop, Polycarp, later writing him a personal letter. Polycarp, born around 69 CE, led this congregation for decades before his own execution in the city's stadium. By 117 CE Smyrna was already a recognized center of orthodoxy in Roman Asia.
properties.image_credit: Agora of ancient Smyrna, Izmir · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the agora of ancient Smyrna

properties.name: Philippi
properties.one_line: Philippi became the first Christian community founded on European soil when Paul baptized the merchant Lydia around 50 CE. A Roman colony strung along the Via Egnatia trade road, the city gave Paul's letter to its congregation an unusually warm, personal tone. Ignatius of Antioch's own letters passed through Philippi around 107 CE, and its bishop later collected copies for Polycarp in Smyrna. The community endured as a stronghold of Pauline Christianity into the second century.
properties.image_credit: Archaeological site of ancient Philippi · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of ancient Philippi, Greece

properties.name: Thessaloniki
properties.one_line: Paul founded this congregation around 50 CE after only a few weeks of preaching, then wrote what may be the earliest surviving Christian text to its Jewish and Greek converts. His first letter praised their courage under harassment; a jealous crowd had already dragged one host before the city's magistrates. Thessalonica's spot on the Via Egnatia kept it in close contact with Rome and Corinth. By 117 CE its believers had outlasted two generations of persecution.
properties.image_credit: Roman Forum of Thessaloniki · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman Forum of ancient Thessalonica

properties.name: Jerusalem
properties.one_line: Jerusalem's first Christians, led by James the brother of Jesus, formed the mother church that Paul and Peter both answered to in the movement's earliest years. Rome besieged and destroyed the city in 70 CE, killing or scattering its population. Later church historians recorded that believers had fled beforehand across the Jordan River to Pella. By 117 CE Jerusalem itself lay in ruins, with no rebuilt city standing until Hadrian founded a colony there after 130 CE.
properties.image_credit: Temple Mount, Jerusalem · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Aerial view of the Temple Mount in Jerusalem

properties.name: Samsun
properties.one_line: Governor Pliny the Younger wrote Trajan around 112 CE asking how to handle the growing number of Christians in this province, the earliest outside account of Christian worship. Pliny reported that accused believers met before dawn to sing hymns and share a meal, then dispersed peacefully. He noted temples had emptied as the new faith spread through cities and countryside alike. Trajan's reply, ordering Pliny to punish only those formally denounced, became imperial policy for decades.
properties.image_credit: Black Sea coast of Pontus, northern Turkey · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Black Sea coastline near ancient Pontus and Bithynia

properties.name: Alexandria
properties.one_line: Alexandria's Jewish community filled two of the city's five districts, the largest Jewish population outside Judaea. Philo, writing in the 30s CE, described its Greek-speaking members worshipping from the Septuagint. The Kitos War erupted here in 115 CE, and by the time Trajan's general Quintus Marcius Turbo crushed the revolt in 117 CE, this ancient community lay devastated. Alexandria's synagogues, once so vast they inspired a Jewish proverb about their size, took generations to recover.
properties.image_credit: Catacombs of Kom El Shoqafa, Roman-period Alexandria · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman-era catacombs in Alexandria, Egypt

properties.name: Rome
properties.one_line: Jewish merchants and freed slaves settled across the Tiber in Trastevere by the second century BCE, Rome's oldest diaspora community. Julius Caesar granted the community formal protections, and by the first century CE it supported multiple synagogues serving thousands. Claudius expelled agitating Jews from Rome around 49 CE, a move Suetonius linked to disputes over a figure named Chrestus. The Arch of Titus, dedicated in 81 CE, displayed the Temple's captured menorah as a permanent trophy.
properties.image_credit: Menorah relief, Arch of Titus, Rome · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Relief of the Jerusalem Temple menorah on the Arch of Titus

properties.name: Cyrene
properties.one_line: Cyrene's Jewish community dated to the Ptolemaic era and won legal equality from Augustus and Agrippa around 14 BCE, recorded on a stone inscribed with five imperial edicts. A separate Jewish politeuma with its own archons governed nearby Berenice by 24 CE. In 115 CE this community launched the opening revolt of the Kitos War under a leader named Lukuas, marching on Alexandria and burning temples along the way. Rome's suppression by 117 CE ended organized Jewish life here for a generation.
properties.image_credit: Archaeological site of Cyrene, Libya · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the ancient city of Cyrene

properties.name: Antioch
properties.one_line: Antioch's Jewish community was old enough that Josephus called it one of the largest in the diaspora, with roots reaching back to the city's founding under the Seleucids. Its members won bronze tablets recording their civic privileges, kept on public display. Antioch avoided the worst of the Kitos War violence that tore through Cyrenaica, Egypt, and Cyprus in 115-117 CE. Its synagogue and Jewish quarter kept functioning through Trajan's reign undisturbed.
properties.image_credit: Mosaic from Roman Antioch · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ancient mosaic from the ruins of Antioch

properties.name: Sardis
properties.one_line: Sardis had Jewish residents since the Persian period, and a Roman decree cited by Josephus confirmed their right to assemble and keep their own laws by 49 BCE. The community held a recognized meeting place for over 150 years before 117 CE, long before its synagogue hall was carved from the city's Roman gymnasium in the third century. Inscriptions from the site number more than eighty in Greek, evidence of a wealthy congregation. Sardis remains the largest Jewish site known from antiquity.
properties.image_credit: Sardis Synagogue site, Lydia, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of the synagogue complex at Sardis

properties.name: Delos
properties.one_line: A building on Delos's eastern shore, raised as early as 150 BCE, is identified by most excavators as one of the oldest Jewish meeting halls outside Judaea. Excavators found a marble seat known as the Throne of Moses against its back wall, alongside dedications to God Most High. The structure sat apart from Delos's crowded harbor district, facing east toward Jerusalem. By 117 CE the community had worshipped on this spot for over two centuries.
properties.image_credit: Archaeological site of ancient Delos · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins on the island of Delos

properties.name: Ostia
properties.one_line: Ostia's Jewish community organized around a synagogue near the city walls, serving Rome's busy port from at least the first century CE onward. Excavators found a marble screen carved with menorahs, a shofar, and a citron, among the clearest Jewish symbols found anywhere in the western Mediterranean. Dockworkers and merchants passing through Ostia linked this congregation to Jewish communities across the empire. The building stayed in use as a synagogue for over four centuries.
properties.image_credit: Menorah relief, Ostia Synagogue · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Menorah carving at the ancient synagogue of Ostia

properties.name: Pozzuoli
properties.one_line: Josephus described a Jewish colony already settled at Puteoli under its older name, Dicaearchia, and used the port himself to reach Rome in the 60s CE. Funerary inscriptions near the city name a gerusiarch, a leader of Jewish elders who maintained the community's burial ground. One tombstone commemorated Claudia Aster, a twenty-five-year-old captive from Jerusalem sold into slavery after 70 CE. Puteoli's harbor was the first Italian soil many Jewish travelers, Paul included, ever touched.
properties.image_credit: Macellum (market) of ancient Puteoli, Pozzuoli · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the Roman market of Puteoli

properties.name: Alexandria
properties.one_line: Isis worship began at Alexandria's founding and by 117 CE anchored one of the ancient world's most influential cults. Sailors credited Isis Pharia, guardian of the harbor beside the great lighthouse, and inscriptions record a shrine built near the Pharos itself. Ptolemy I created the linked cult of Serapis here to unite Greek and Egyptian worshippers under one divine pair. From this city, devotion to Isis spread to Rome, Pompeii, and Delos within two centuries.
properties.image_credit: Serapeum of Alexandria, home of the city's Egyptian cults · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of the Serapeum at Alexandria

properties.name: Pompeii
properties.one_line: Pompeii's Temple of Isis arrived around 100 BCE and stood until Vesuvius buried the city in 79 CE, thirty-eight years before this map's date. An earthquake in 62 CE had already damaged the shrine, and a freedman named Numerius Popidius Ampliatus paid to rebuild it in his son's name. Excavators in 1764 found it still standing with painted walls intact, the first religious building unearthed at Pompeii. Its frescoes gave eighteenth-century Europe its first look at a Roman mystery cult in ruins.
properties.image_credit: Fresco of Io and Isis from the Temple of Isis, Pompeii · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Fresco from the Temple of Isis at Pompeii, buried in 79 CE

properties.name: Rome
properties.one_line: The Senate first vowed a temple to Isis and Serapis in the Campus Martius in 43 BCE, giving the cult an official foothold in the city. Fire destroyed it in 80 CE, and Domitian rebuilt it on a lavish scale. Its precinct held genuine Egyptian obelisks, sphinxes, and granite columns carved with priests holding canopic jars, later dragged across Rome to decorate Renaissance piazzas. By 117 CE the Iseum Campense was the largest Isis temple in the western Mediterranean.
properties.image_credit: Sphinx from the Iseum Campense, Musei Capitolini, Rome · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Egyptian-style sphinx sculpture from Rome's Temple of Isis and Serapis

properties.name: Delos
properties.one_line: Egyptian traders brought Isis worship to Delos by the third century BCE, and the island produced more dedications to Egyptian gods than anywhere outside Egypt. Three linked sanctuaries rose on a terrace above the island's reservoir, the largest covering some six thousand square meters with temples to Isis, Serapis, and Anubis. Worshippers abstained from wine inside the precinct, following rules imported from Egypt. The sanctuaries kept functioning even as Delos's slave market faded after 88 BCE.
properties.image_credit: Sanctuary of the Egyptian gods, Delos · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of the temples to Isis and other Egyptian gods on Delos

properties.name: Rome
properties.one_line: Rome imported Cybele's sacred black stone from Anatolia in 204 BCE on a Sibylline oracle's promise it would help defeat Hannibal. The Senate dedicated a full temple to her on the Palatine in 191 BCE, making Cybele the first eastern deity granted official Roman state cult status. Her spring festival, the Megalesia, filled Rome's calendar with games for over a week every April. By 117 CE the cult had stood at the city's religious center for over three centuries.
properties.image_credit: Palatine Hill, Rome, site of the Temple of Magna Mater · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins on the Palatine Hill in Rome

properties.name: Pessinus
properties.one_line: Pessinus was Cybele's original home shrine, the Anatolian sanctuary that supplied Rome with her sacred stone in 204 BCE. Galatian tribes ruled the surrounding highlands by the second century BCE, yet the temple kept drawing pilgrims from across Asia Minor. Tiberius financed a new temple on the site between 25 and 35 CE, rebuilding Pessinus as a Greco-Roman city around its ancient cult. By 117 CE the sanctuary remained the mother-shrine for every Cybele temple in the empire.
properties.image_credit: Reconstruction of the Cybele temple at Pessinus · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 3D reconstruction of the temple complex at Pessinus

properties.name: Ostia
properties.one_line: Cybele's cult reached Ostia by the first century CE, taking root in a triangular field inside the city walls called the Campo della Magna Mater. Worshippers there also kept a shrine to Attis, the god's mythical consort, and a corps of lance-bearing priests called Hastiferi who danced in processions. Initiation rites reportedly included the taurobolium, a bull sacrifice whose blood was sprinkled over devotees. Ostia's role as Rome's port made this field a gateway for eastern cults entering Italy.
properties.image_credit: Relief depicting a sacrifice to Cybele, Ostia Antica · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ancient relief of a sacrifice to Cybele found at Ostia

properties.name: Eleusis
properties.one_line: The Eleusinian Mysteries initiated worshippers into secret rites of Demeter and Persephone from the second millennium BCE, promising a better fate after death. Roman citizens sought initiation as eagerly as Greeks did; Cicero and Augustus both reportedly underwent it. Hadrian's rebuilding of the sanctuary began only a few years after 117 CE, but its Telesterion initiation hall was already centuries old by this date. No initiate could describe what happened inside, on pain of death.
properties.image_credit: Sanctuary of Demeter and Kore and the Telesterion, Eleusis · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The Telesterion initiation hall at the sanctuary of Eleusis

properties.name: Samothrace
properties.one_line: The Sanctuary of the Great Gods on Samothrace hosted mystery rites honoring the Kabeiroi, deities whose true names initiates were forbidden to speak. Unlike Eleusis, initiation here was open to anyone regardless of citizenship, gender, or status, one of antiquity's most inclusive rites. The Arsinoeion, a rotunda funded by Ptolemaic queen Arsinoe II, still dominated the sanctuary's skyline by 117 CE. Sailors credited the cult's twin gods with power to calm storms at sea.
properties.image_credit: The Arsinoeion, Sanctuary of the Great Gods, Samothrace · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of the Arsinoeion rotunda at the Samothrace sanctuary

properties.name: Magnesia on the Maeander
properties.one_line: Ignatius of Antioch wrote to this congregation around 107 CE while being marched to Rome under armed guard, urging its members to submit to their young bishop Damas despite his age. He praised Magnesia's Christians for sending a delegation to meet him at Smyrna, a gesture that moved him to write back at length. The city sat twelve miles from Ephesus along the Maeander valley trade route, keeping it in close contact with the region's other churches. Ignatius warned the community against slipping back into Jewish practice, a sign the two faiths still overlapped here in daily life.
properties.image_credit: Reconstructed temple facade from Magnesia on the Maeander, Pergamon Museum, Berlin · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Reconstructed temple facade fragments from ancient Magnesia on the Maeander

properties.name: Tralles
properties.one_line: Ignatius of Antioch addressed a letter to Tralles around 107 CE, thanking its bishop Polybius for traveling to Smyrna to visit him in chains. He urged the community to stay under its bishop's authority and warned against docetist teachers who denied Christ had suffered in the flesh. Tralles sat inland from Ephesus on the Roman road through the Maeander valley, a Hellenistic city with its own gymnasium and public baths. Ignatius signed off certain he would die in Rome, asking the Trallians to pray for the church in Syria he left behind.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of ancient Tralles, Aydin · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Alasehir
properties.one_line: The Book of Revelation praised Philadelphia's Christians around 95 CE as the only one of the seven churches to receive no criticism, promising them an open door no one could shut. Ignatius of Antioch passed through the city around 107 CE and later wrote back warning against a faction that had tried to divide the congregation during his visit. Founded in the second century BCE and prone to earthquakes, Philadelphia's Christians met in a city Roman writers already described as constantly rebuilding after tremors. Its name and its church both survived antiquity, giving Philadelphia a continuous Christian presence longer than almost any other city on this list.
properties.image_credit: Site of biblical Philadelphia, Alasehir, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Modern view of Alasehir, ancient Philadelphia, one of the seven churches of Revelation

properties.name: Pergamon
properties.one_line: Revelation's letter to Pergamon around 95 CE called the city the place "where Satan's throne is," likely a reference to its towering altar of Zeus or its role as a seat of the imperial cult. The text names a martyr, Antipas, killed there before this date, one of the earliest individual Christians recorded outside the apostolic circle. Pergamon served as the seat of Rome's provincial governor in Asia and hosted one of the ancient world's largest libraries, rivaling Alexandria's own. Its small Christian minority worshipped in the shadow of the Asclepion, a healing sanctuary that drew pilgrims from across the Mediterranean.
properties.image_credit: Acropolis of ancient Pergamon, Bergama, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins on the acropolis of ancient Pergamon

properties.name: Thyatira
properties.one_line: Revelation singled out Thyatira's church around 95 CE for tolerating a female prophet the text calls "Jezebel," who taught believers they could eat food sacrificed to idols. The city ran on its trade guilds, especially its purple-dye workers, the same trade that later gave the New Testament merchant Lydia her livelihood in Philippi. Thyatira sat on the road linking Pergamon to Sardis, a modest garrison town refounded by the Seleucids around 281 BCE. Its small Christian community left no other surviving written record from the century after Revelation was composed.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of ancient Thyatira, Akhisar · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Sardis
properties.one_line: Revelation's letter to Sardis around 95 CE accused its Christians of being spiritually dead behind a living reputation, urging the few who had "not soiled their garments" to stay watchful. The city had been sacked by surprise attack twice in its history, a memory the text invokes when it warns believers Christ would come "like a thief" if they failed to wake up. Sardis's ancient wealth, built on gold panned from the Pactolus River under the Lydian kings, had faded by Roman times into a comfortable provincial capital. Its small Christian congregation shared the city with one of the largest and best-documented Jewish communities in the entire diaspora.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Artemis at Sardis · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the Temple of Artemis at ancient Sardis

properties.name: Laodicea
properties.one_line: Revelation delivered its harshest rebuke to Laodicea around 95 CE, condemning its church as "lukewarm" and boasting of riches while spiritually poor and blind. Paul's letter to the Colossians, written a generation earlier, instructed that the letter be passed on and read aloud in Laodicea too, showing the two congregations already exchanged correspondence. The city rebuilt itself after a devastating earthquake in 60 CE without asking Rome for financial aid, a point of civic pride Revelation's author seems to mock. Laodicea's banking houses and famous black wool trade made it one of Phrygia's wealthiest cities by 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Central Bath Complex, Laodicea on the Lycus, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the Roman bath complex at ancient Laodicea

properties.name: Colossae
properties.one_line: Paul's letter to the Colossians, written around 60 CE, addressed a small congregation founded not by Paul himself but by his associate Epaphras, a native of the city. The letter argued against local teachings blending angel worship, dietary rules, and ascetic practice that Paul warned were leading the church astray. A major earthquake struck the Lycus Valley around the same decade, and by the time Revelation named the region's churches thirty years later, neighboring Laodicea had eclipsed Colossae as the valley's leading city. Colossae's mound has never been formally excavated, leaving its Christian community's fate after 117 CE largely unrecorded.
properties.image_credit: View from the mound of ancient Colossae toward Honaz, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: View from the unexcavated mound of ancient Colossae

properties.name: Troas
properties.one_line: Paul raised a young man named Eutychus from the dead in Troas after he fell from a third-story window during an all-night sermon, an episode Acts places around 57 CE. Ignatius of Antioch reached the city around 107 CE under armed guard and used the stopover to dictate three more letters, to Philadelphia, Smyrna, and Polycarp, before soldiers hurried him onto a ship for Macedonia. Troas's harbor made it the main crossing point between Asia Minor and Macedonia, a route both Paul and Ignatius depended on for their journeys. The city would later host a large gymnasium and bath complex funded by Herodes Atticus, built decades after Ignatius passed through in chains.
properties.image_credit: Bath complex near ancient Alexandria Troas · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the Roman bath complex at Alexandria Troas

properties.name: Kechries
properties.one_line: Paul's letter to the Romans, written around 57 CE, commended Phoebe, a deaconess of the church at Cenchreae, entrusting her to carry the letter itself to Rome. Cenchreae served as Corinth's eastern port on the Saronic Gulf, roughly six miles from the city center, linking this small congregation to sea traffic from Ephesus and beyond. Paul himself had his hair cut here under a vow before sailing for Syria, a detail Acts records around 52 CE. The port's mixed population of sailors, merchants, and dockworkers gave this small congregation an unusually cosmopolitan reach for its size.
properties.image_credit: Roman-period tomb at ancient Cenchreae, Corinth's eastern port · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman monumental tomb at the archaeological site of Cenchreae

properties.name: Acmonia
properties.one_line: Around 100 CE, a wealthy citizen of Acmonia named Julia Severa funded the construction of a synagogue building, an act later commemorated by an inscription the community's elders set up in gratitude. Julia Severa herself served as a high priestess of the imperial cult, showing how thoroughly Jewish and civic life intertwined in this Phrygian town. The inscription names three synagogue officials by title, rare evidence for how a diaspora congregation organized itself outside the empire's major cities. Acmonia's Jewish community endured for generations afterward, leaving behind some of Asia Minor's richest funerary inscriptions.
properties.image_credit: Julia Severa synagogue inscription, Acmonia · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Inscription recording Julia Severa's construction of the Acmonia synagogue

properties.name: Benghazi
properties.one_line: An inscription dated to 13 BCE names nine Jewish archons who governed Berenice's community as a self-organized politeuma, answering to their own elected officials rather than a single ethnarch. A second inscription from 56 CE records the community's thanks to donors who helped fund and repair its synagogue building. Most of the names honored in both texts are Greek rather than Hebrew, pointing to a highly Hellenized congregation active in civic life. Berenice sat roughly 120 miles east of Cyrene, giving Roman Cyrenaica two separately organized Jewish communities within the same province.

properties.name: Hierapolis
properties.one_line: Jewish settlers reportedly arrived in Hierapolis under a resettlement policy of the Seleucid king Antiochos III around 200 BCE, planting a community that outlasted his dynasty by centuries. A funerary inscription from the city's necropolis specifies fines to be paid to "the group of Jews residing in Hierapolis" if a family tomb went undisturbed, evidence the community held recognized legal standing. Local trade guilds, including the purple-dyers and carpet-weavers, took on obligations to decorate Jewish graves at Passover and Pentecost, a rare glimpse of Jewish and pagan guild life overlapping. Most of the surviving grave inscriptions naming this community date to the second and third centuries, closer to but after this map's 117 CE snapshot.
properties.image_credit: Necropolis of ancient Hierapolis, Pamukkale, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Tombs in the necropolis of ancient Hierapolis, where Jewish grave inscriptions were found

properties.name: Nehardea
properties.one_line: Nehardea's Jewish settlers traced their community's founding to exiles deported from Jerusalem under King Jehoiachin in the sixth century BCE, who reportedly built its synagogue from stones carried out of the fallen Temple itself. Two brothers from the city, Anilai and Asinai, carved out a semi-autonomous Jewish state on the Euphrates in the 20s CE under Parthian sovereignty, an episode the historian Josephus recorded in detail. Around 117 CE, the rabbi Akiva traveled to Nehardea to set the Jewish calendar, confirming the city's standing as a recognized center of religious authority. Nehardea sat outside the Roman Empire's eastern frontier, inside Parthian territory, making it a neighbor of Trajan's empire rather than a subject of it.

properties.name: Pisidian Antioch
properties.one_line: Acts places Paul and Barnabas preaching in Pisidian Antioch's synagogue around 47 CE, where Paul's sermon on Jesus as the promised Messiah split the audience between eager converts and furious opponents. Local synagogue leaders, unable to silence Paul themselves, enlisted the city's leading women and officials to have him expelled from the region entirely. The city served as the Roman colonia and administrative capital of the Pisidian district, home to a large resident Jewish population by the time Paul arrived. Its synagogue predated Rome's colonial refoundation of the city under Augustus, giving the community deep local roots by 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of ancient Pisidian Antioch, Yalvac, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Panoramic view of the ruins of Pisidian Antioch

properties.name: Salamis
properties.one_line: Acts records Paul, Barnabas, and the Cypriot-born John Mark preaching in "the synagogues of the Jews" at Salamis around 45 CE, using the plural to describe a community large enough to fill more than one building. Cyprus held one of the diaspora's most substantial Jewish populations by the early second century, concentrated heavily around this port city on the island's east coast. In 116 CE Cypriot Jews rose up under a leader named Artemion during the empire-wide Kitos War, and ancient accounts claim tens of thousands died in the fighting that followed. Rome's suppression by 117 CE was so severe that Jews were reportedly barred from setting foot on Cyprus afterward, ending organized Jewish life on the island for generations.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of ancient Salamis, Cyprus · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Archaeological ruins at ancient Salamis, Cyprus

properties.name: Kechries
properties.one_line: Excavators in the 1960s uncovered a temple on the southwest edge of Cenchreae's ancient harbor that many identify as the very sanctuary the novelist Apuleius described his hero Lucius entering as a new initiate of Isis. In Apuleius's account, set in this port, the goddess appeared to the transformed Lucius rising from the sea and instructed him how to become human again during her spring festival, the Navigium Isidis. Cenchreae served as Corinth's gateway to the eastern Mediterranean, a natural landing point for cults arriving from Egypt and the Levant. Isis worship at this harbor likely predates Apuleius's account by generations, riding the same trade routes that carried grain ships from Alexandria.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Isis at the ancient harbor of Cenchreae, Greece · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of the Temple of Isis at the harbor of ancient Cenchreae

properties.name: Ostia
properties.one_line: Inscriptions found across Ostia record dedications tied to Isis, worshipped alongside Serapis and the Magna Mater, evidence of an organized Egyptian cult community in Rome's own port city. Despite this rich epigraphic record, the actual Iseum building itself has never been located or excavated, and its exact site along the Tiber remains a matter of scholarly reconstruction. Ostia's excavated Serapeum, a separate temple to the male half of the pair, was formally dedicated on Hadrian's birthday in 127 CE, a decade after this map's snapshot. Sailors and merchants passing through Ostia's harbor kept Egyptian cult practice alive here long before that later building went up.
properties.image_credit: Cult statue, Temple of Roma and Augustus, Ostia · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Soli
properties.one_line: The geographer Strabo, writing around the turn of the era, described a shared sanctuary of Aphrodite and Isis at Soloi, evidence Egyptian cult worship had already merged with the city's older goddess cult by the early Roman period. Excavators later confirmed the site, finding linked precincts naming Isis, Serapis, and the Dioskouroi standing alongside two temples to Aphrodite first raised in the third century BCE. Sculpture recovered from the Aphrodite temple dates to the first century CE, confirming the sanctuary complex stayed in active use under Roman rule. Soloi sat on Cyprus's northwestern coast, one of the island's ten ancient city-kingdoms and a minor hub for cults arriving from Egypt.

properties.name: Acrocorinth
properties.one_line: The traveler Pausanias, touring Corinth in the second century CE, counted two separate precincts of Isis on the slope of Acrocorinth, one dedicated to her as "Pelagian," of the sea, the other to "Egyptian" Isis, alongside two shrines to Serapis. His description records sanctuaries that had stood for generations by his visit, planted after Julius Caesar refounded Corinth as a Roman colony in 44 BCE. Corinth's mixed population of Italian colonists, Greek residents, and Levantine traders made the city one of Achaea's most receptive markets for imported cults. The Egyptian sanctuaries shared Acrocorinth's steep summit with an older, larger temple to Aphrodite, the mountain's most famous shrine.
properties.image_credit: Summit of Acrocorinth, site of Corinth's Isis and Aphrodite sanctuaries · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Summit of Acrocorinth above ancient Corinth

properties.name: Kyzikos
properties.one_line: Ancient tradition credited Kyzikos's cult of the Mother of the Gods to the mythical Argonauts, who supposedly founded her sanctuary on nearby Mount Dindymon during their voyage for the Golden Fleece. The city celebrated her festival with public ceremony grand enough that ancient writers singled it out among Anatolia's leading Cybele cult centers, alongside Pergamon and Pessinus. Kyzikos sat on the Kapidag Peninsula on the Sea of Marmara, a wealthy port city that minted its own celebrated gold coinage for centuries. Within a generation of 117 CE, the city would also raise the largest Greco-Roman temple ever built, dedicated to the emperor Hadrian, on a site already steeped in Cybele's mythology.
properties.image_credit: Ruins at ancient Kyzikos, including the later Temple of Hadrian · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of monumental temple ruins at the site of ancient Kyzikos

properties.name: Sardis
properties.one_line: The historian Herodotus recorded a native cult of Kybebe, a Lydian mother goddess, already established at Sardis when a fire tore through the city's sanctuaries during the Ionian Revolt around 498 BCE. Lydian inscriptions preserve her name centuries before Greek writers began identifying her with the Anatolian Cybele worshipped across the Roman world. Her sanctuary at Sardis has been linked to the gold-refining industry that made the city's Lydian kings famous, tying the goddess to the wealth of the ancient Pactolus riverbed. By 117 CE, Sardis's identity as one of Cybele's oldest and most authentic cult homes had outlasted the Lydian kingdom that first raised her temple by six centuries.
properties.image_credit: Column from the Temple of Artemis at Sardis · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Carved column from the sanctuary area of ancient Sardis

properties.name: Athens
properties.one_line: Athens converted its Old Bouleuterion, the council chamber on the west side of the Agora, into a sanctuary for the Mother of the Gods after a new council house replaced it at the end of the fifth century BCE. According to a founding legend the city told about itself, Athenians killed a wandering priest of Cybele who tried to introduce her worship, and built the Metroon only after the goddess punished the city with plague. The building doubled as Athens's state archive, storing official documents under the goddess's protection for centuries. The Metroon remained a working sanctuary and record hall through the Roman period, still standing in the Agora by 117 CE alongside monuments centuries older than Rome's own arrival in Greece.
properties.image_credit: Remains of the Old Bouleuterion and Metroon, Athens Agora · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Foundations of the Metroon, sanctuary of the Mother of the Gods, in the Athens Agora

properties.name: Athens
properties.one_line: Athenian inscriptions name dozens of initiates into the cult of Sabazios by 100 BCE, a Phrygian sky and fertility god whose nighttime rites involved ritual purification with mud and a sacred drink. Devotees marked their allegiance with small bronze hands, fingers raised in a gesture of blessing and covered with a snake, pinecone, and thunderbolt, meant to be mounted on poles and carried through the streets in procession. The cult had circulated in Athens since at least the fifth century BCE, mocked by the comic playwright Aristophanes for its foreign, ecstatic style of worship. Sabazios worship spread across the Roman world by the early second century CE, reaching from Attica to Britain, carried by soldiers, merchants, and the god's traveling priests.
properties.image_credit: Bronze votive Hand of Sabazius, a ritual object type used across the Roman world, British Museum · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Bronze votive hand associated with the cult of Sabazios

properties.name: Circus Maximus
properties.one_line: Rome's oldest sun cult, Sol Indiges, received an annual public sacrifice every August 9th, a rite ancient tradition credited to the Sabine king Titus Tatius in the city's earliest legendary period. His cult held a shrine on the Quirinal Hill and a separate sanctuary inside the Circus Maximus, where archaeological remains date back to at least the third century BCE. Roman poets equated Sol Indiges with the Greek sun god Helios, but his worship stayed a distinctly homegrown Roman institution, unlike the later Syrian sun cult of Sol Invictus that would not arrive in Rome for another century. By 117 CE, Sol Indiges had already been one of Rome's recognized state gods for centuries, watching over chariot races from his shrine inside the Circus Maximus.
properties.image_credit: The Circus Maximus, Rome, site of a shrine to Sol Indiges · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The Circus Maximus in Rome

properties.name: Villa of the Mysteries
properties.one_line: The Villa of the Mysteries, on Pompeii's northwestern edge, preserves a nearly life-size fresco cycle showing a woman's initiation into the rites of Dionysus, painted around 60 BCE and buried intact when Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE. The frescoes depict flagellation, ecstatic dance, and a reclining Dionysus himself, the most complete surviving visual record of any Greco-Roman mystery cult's initiation ritual. Unlike the more famous Eleusinian Mysteries, Dionysiac cult groups organized privately in villas and associations rather than around one central sanctuary, spreading informally across Italy for over two centuries before Pompeii's destruction. By 117 CE the villa itself had lain buried under volcanic ash for thirty-eight years, but the Dionysiac mystery worship its frescoes recorded continued in cities across the empire.
properties.image_credit: Fresco from the Villa of the Mysteries, Pompeii · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Fresco depicting Dionysiac initiation rites, Villa of the Mysteries, Pompeii

properties.name: Carnuntum
properties.one_line: A centurion of the Fifteenth Legion raised a stone altar to Mithras on this Danube frontier, the oldest securely dated Mithraic dedication in the Roman West. His unit shipped out for Trajan's Parthian war in 114 CE and never came back, which pins the altar to before that year. Soldiers who fought Parthians and Jews in the East carried the cult home to this Pannonian garrison town. The inscription reads simply: to unconquered Mithras, a vow fulfilled.
properties.image_credit: The Heidentor, Carnuntum · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Kerch
properties.one_line: Bosporan Jews freed their slaves inside this city's synagogue and had the ceremony carved in stone, dated by the reigning king's regnal year like a notarized deed. One such manumission, overseen by the congregation, survives from 81 CE. The community used the Greek word proseuche for its prayer house, the same term diaspora synagogues used from Egypt to Rome. Six such inscriptions place a working Jewish congregation on the empire's northern edge decades before Trajan died.

properties.name: Bodrum
properties.one_line: The city council granted its Jewish residents, men and women alike, the right to keep the Sabbath and build a prayer house by the sea, a decree the historian Josephus later copied word for word. The proseuche stood on the waterfront, matching the diaspora custom of praying near water. That civic guarantee outlasted the Hellenistic kings who granted it and still governed the community under Roman rule. Jewish elders kept citing the decree to later officials as legal proof of their rights.
properties.image_credit: The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, Bodrum · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Ephesus
properties.one_line: Roman citizens who happened to be Jewish got pulled off a legionary conscription roll here in 49 BCE, exempted because the consul honored their ancestral rights. Marcus Agrippa later guaranteed Ephesian Jews could send temple donations to Jerusalem and keep the Sabbath undisturbed. Josephus copied several of the city's decrees into his own history as legal precedent. Their tombstones, carved in Greek like everyone else's in this Hellenized port, show a community fully at home in the city.
properties.image_credit: The Odeon of Ephesus · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Tocra
properties.one_line: Greek epitaphs mark this Cyrenaican port's Jewish graves right through the Flavian decades, part of the four-city Jewish settlement Strabo described across the Libyan Pentapolis. Then the evidence stops. The Jewish revolt of 115 to 117 CE tore through Cyrenaica under a leader named Lukuas, and Roman troops crushed it by slaughtering the very communities that started it, Tocra's included. Trajan died that August with the region's synagogues and Jewish population largely wiped out.

properties.name: Laodicea
properties.one_line: A Roman governor tried to seize the annual gold this city's Jews collected for the Jerusalem Temple, and Cicero's courtroom defense of him is the reason the sum is still on record. The seizure exposed a large, organized, tax-paying Jewish population functioning openly under Roman law. That same fundraising network kept sending contributions every year until the Temple fell in 70 CE. Wool merchants and Jewish elders shared a marketplace in a city famous across the empire for its black fleece.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/The Central Bath Complex, Laodicea on the Lycus, Phrygia, Turkey (32067205746).jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Central Bath Complex, Laodicea on the Lycus · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Apamea
properties.one_line: A Roman governor confiscated roughly a hundred pounds of gold from this Syrian city's Jewish community in 62 BCE, money members had spent a year collecting for Jerusalem. Cicero defended the seizure in court, and his surviving speech is the only reason the sum is known at all. That kind of organized, empire-wide fundraising kept running for communities like Apamea's for over a century after. The city sat astride the Orontes at a strategic river crossing, good ground for merchants to prosper.

properties.name: Kos
properties.one_line: A Roman consul once wrote to this Aegean island naming its Jewish community among a dozen others under official Roman protection, a letter Josephus later preserved word for word. Herod the Great, a client king with money to spend, personally funded the island's gymnasium and kept close ties to its elite. Jewish islanders here traded, worshipped, and buried their dead within sight of the harbor for generations. Later communities kept citing that letter as proof of their standing.
properties.image_credit: Ancient Agora of Kos · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: London
properties.one_line: Someone scratched 'Londini ad fanum Isidis', at the temple of Isis, London, into a clay wine jug dropped near London Bridge in the first century CE. It is the earliest surviving instance of the city's name in any written record. The temple itself has never been found, but a later inscription confirms a Roman governor rebuilt it after it collapsed from age, proving it stood for generations. London remains the only place in Roman Britain with evidence of Isis worship at all.
properties.image_credit: The London Wall, Londinium · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Baelo Claudia
properties.one_line: Fishermen in this tuna-salting boomtown on the Strait of Gibraltar built Isis her own temple beside the city's Capitoline gods, a rare honor in Roman Spain. A votive inscription on its steps records a local man, Marcus Sempronius Maximus, fulfilling a vow to Isis the Lady. Sailors favored her as patron of safe voyages, fitting a town whose economy ran on garum and tuna shipped across dangerous water. It remains the only Isis temple in Spain with its ground plan still intact.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of Baelo Claudia · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Thessaloniki
properties.one_line: This sanctuary to Serapis, Isis, and Anubis had stood for centuries by Trajan's reign, built soon after the city itself was founded around 315 BCE. A 1917 fire accidentally uncovered more than seventy buried Greek inscriptions, most dedicated to Osiris or Isis, alongside statues and a crypt reached by an underground tunnel. Egyptian merchants likely carried the cult here along the trade routes that made the city rich, and worship continued for five centuries straight.
properties.image_credit: Roman Forum of Thessalonica · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Gortyn
properties.one_line: A local Cretan woman paid to rebuild this older sanctuary to Isis, Serapis, and Anubis right around Trajan's reign, and had her generosity carved in stone by the entrance. Three separate niches inside held statues of the three gods side by side, above a hidden underground chamber reached by its own staircase. It is the only Egyptian-cult sanctuary ever excavated on Crete. The building sat beside Gortyn's Temple of Apollo, putting Egyptian and Greek gods on the same sacred street.
properties.image_credit: Roman Odeon of Gortyna, Crete · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Nemi
properties.one_line: Runaway slaves could become high priest here by killing the man who already held the job, a duel fought under one sacred oak for over five centuries. The winner took the title King of the Wood, guarding a shrine to Diana of Nemi that drew pilgrims to this crater lake since around 300 BCE. Worshippers threw thousands of model body parts and terracotta babies into the sacred spring, begging for healing or safe childbirth. Emperors left dedications here without ending the priest-killing custom.

properties.name: Manbij
properties.one_line: Two colossal phalli flanked the north gate of Atargatis's temple here, where sacred fish swam in a pool pilgrims were forbidden to touch. The Syrian Goddess ruled fertility and protection from a sanctuary so wealthy the writer Lucian devoted a whole treatise to its rituals. Self-castrated priests called galli danced into ecstatic frenzies during her festivals, fascinating Greek and Roman visitors. The cult had flourished for generations by the time Trajan marched past toward Parthia.

properties.name: Palmyra
properties.one_line: An inscription in the cella wall dates this desert temple's consecration to a precise year, 32 CE, nearly a century before Trajan died. Bel shared the sanctuary with a moon god and a sun god, a triad letting Palmyrene merchants worship ancestral gods behind a Greco-Roman facade. Caravan wealth from overland trade paid for decades of ongoing construction, adding courtyards and columns into the second century. Palmyra's merchant elite treated the temple as a monument to their own fortune.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Bel, Palmyra · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Doliche
properties.one_line: Priests had sacrificed to a storm god on this hilltop since roughly 1000 BCE, a millennium of worship by the time Rome absorbed Commagene in 30 BCE. Romans renamed him Jupiter Dolichenus but kept his old iconography nearly unchanged, an armored figure standing on a bull with a lightning bolt in hand. Soldiers on this Syrian frontier carried the cult home, planting his shrines as far as Britain and the Danube. The sanctuary itself stayed in continuous use for roughly 1,300 years.
properties.image_credit: Votive statuette of Jupiter Dolichenus, found at Carnuntum — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Palestrina
properties.one_line: Priests here practiced one of Italy's oldest forms of divination, drawing wooden lots called sortes for pilgrims consulting Fortuna's oracle. Her sanctuary climbed the hillside in seven terraces, one of the largest religious complexes in the Roman world after being rebuilt following Sulla's sack of the city in 82 BCE. Julius Caesar's own family claimed personal devotion to Fortuna Primigenia. The complex doubled as a bank, since Romans trusted temples to guard deposits nobody dared steal.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Palestrina - Santuario della Fortuna Primigenia - vista della rampa di sinistra.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia, Palestrina · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Lucus Feroniae
properties.one_line: Slaves who reached this grove and sat on one stone seat inside the temple stood up free, their masters bound by custom to manumit them on the spot. Feronia was an old Italic goddess of freedmen and wild groves, worshipped here before Rome conquered the surrounding Sabine and Faliscan lands. The sanctuary mattered enough that Augustus founded a veteran colony around it, named after her own grove. Merchants gathered at her annual fair, mixing trade with freedom rites under the trees.

properties.name: Baalbek
properties.one_line: Trajan stopped here in 115 CE, en route to invade Parthia, to consult the sanctuary's famous oracle about the campaign's odds. Priests read omens tied to an ancient Semitic sky god the Romans called Jupiter Heliopolitanus, worshipped here long before Rome reached Syria. Augustus had planted a veteran colony nearby and funded a platform built from stones weighing hundreds of tons each. The sanctuary kept growing for two more centuries into one of the largest religious complexes in the empire.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Jupiter, Baalbek · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Bergama
properties.one_line: Sabazios worship spread through the Roman world largely from this city, where inscriptions name his priesthood a civic office, not a fringe cult. Worshippers carried small bronze hands cast in a blessing gesture, covered with tiny pine cones, snakes, and turtles, mounted on staffs for processions. The god fused Phrygian and Thracian sky-father traditions with wine rites, prompting Greeks to compare him to a foreign Dionysus. Dedications here run continuously from the late first century CE.
properties.image_credit: Acropolis of ancient Pergamon · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Rome
properties.one_line: A Roman praetor expelled Sabazios worshippers from the city in 139 BCE, lumping them with astrologers and Jews as a foreign influence, per the historian Valerius Maximus. The crackdown did not work. Bronze votive hands cast in a blessing gesture and dedicated to Sabazios turn up across Italy from the imperial period, proof the cult kept quietly running for centuries after. Immigrants from Phrygia and Thrace kept his mystery rites alive on Rome's margins.
